title: Algebraic extinction in acyclic spreading models: explicit counterexamples, genericity and support-checkable repairs
shortTitle: When an outbreak ends on the tipping point
oneLine: A successor to an earlier Evidence Press refutation of the Chan–Crommelin–Mandjes exponential-extinction conjecture: a four-compartment spreading model with both graphs acyclic fades like t^(-3/2) with an exact solution, nothing slower is possible with four compartments, and such slow tails need finely tuned starts and can be ruled out by checkable conditions.
abstract: Chan, Crommelin and Mandjes conjectured that, in their class of interaction-driven spreading models, every vanishing compartment decays exponentially whenever two graphs built from the model are acyclic or nearly so. An earlier Evidence Press release (doi:10.5281/zenodo.23501636) refuted this conjecture with a four-compartment model decaying like 18/t², proved four compartments necessary and gave a spectral repair. This successor explains the mechanism: an endgame in which the effective reproduction number of the active compartment tends to exactly one. It gives a four-compartment staged-rumour model in which both graphs are acyclic and the trajectory is explicit, with activity x(t) ~ √(3/8) t^(−3/2), and a second example decaying like 4t^(−2) that needs less tuning; within the source's encoding of recovery, a no-direct-infection SWIR-type submodel also admits a t^(−3/2) counterexample. With four compartments no tail is slower than t^(−3/2), and chains give t^(−1−1/m) for every even m. Algebraic extinction requires non-generic initial data whenever the fluxes share one active catalyst, a general law gives how fast exponential decay returns after a perturbation, the slow tails never follow an outbreak peak in the chain, SWIR and hierarchy families, and support- and rate-checkable conditions guarantee exponential decay. An exploratory simulation suggests finite populations die out much earlier. AI-assisted, unrefereed candidate; no external peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification is claimed.

keyResults: Successor result: the conjecture was first refuted by the earlier release (18/t², cyclic dependency graph); here both graphs are acyclic and the trajectory is explicit, x(t) ~ √(3/8) t^(−3/2), with R_eff → 1 and 1 − R_eff ~ 9/(2t) (Theorem 3.1, proof; exact).

A no-direct-infection SWIR-type submodel of the Janssen–Müller–Stenull generalised epidemic process, with recovery encoded as in the source, is in the class and gives a t^(−3/2) counterexample at a tricritical-type triple zero (§3.4, proof; exact).

Limits: three compartments never suffice (as in the earlier release); any four-compartment model decays exponentially, like t^(−2) or like t^(−3/2), so nothing is slower (Theorem 5.7, proof); chains give t^(−1−1/m) for every even m (Theorem 5.1).

Fragility: algebraic extinction lies on a null set of starting points in single-catalyst models (codimensions 1 and 2 in the chain; Theorem 6.2), exponential decay returns after perturbation with rate ∝ |ε|^((k−1)/k) (Theorem 6.3), and no outbreak peak precedes a slow tail in the chain, SWIR and hierarchy families (Proposition 6.5).

Repairs: the log-rate equals the spectral abscissa of the limiting Metzler block (same statement as the earlier release), and support- and rate-checkable conditions guarantee exponential decay (Corollaries 7.3–7.4, proof). Finite populations die out at about 1.5 N^0.42 (exploratory).

narration: When an outbreak ends on the tipping point. An Evidence Press briefing. Epidemics, rumours, opinions and new habits all spread from person to person. Compartment models describe this by splitting a population into a few groups, such as unaware, heard it once, spreading and lost interest, and tracking how people move between them. In the classic epidemic model the last spreaders fade away exponentially: their number falls by a fixed fraction every day. In 2025, Chan, Crommelin and Mandjes conjectured that this always happens in a broad class of such models, provided two diagrams describing who can move where, and who depends on whom, contain no loops. That conjecture had already been refuted, by an earlier Evidence Press release published the day before this one, with a four-group model that fades like one over time squared. This release is its successor. It explains why the conjecture fails. Fading is exponential when the outbreak overshoots, so that each spreader ends up replacing less than one of itself. If instead the endgame lands exactly on the tipping point, where each spreader replaces exactly one, the fade-out becomes a slow power law. The release gives a four-group staged rumour model in which both diagrams have no loops, writes down its whole trajectory exactly, and shows that its spreaders fade like time to the power minus three halves. A version of a well-known two-step contagion model from the physics literature does the same. With four groups nothing fades more slowly than that. The slow tails are fragile. They need finely tuned starting points, a small nudge restores exponential decay at a predictable rate, and in the families studied they never follow an outbreak peak. Simple conditions on the model rule them out altogether. For epidemiology, slow fade-out is the signature of an endgame poised at the tipping point. But a simulation suggests real, finite populations die out much earlier than the smooth model predicts. This is an anonymous, AI-assisted, unrefereed candidate, not peer reviewed or independently reproduced. Published on 21 October 2026, its paper and evidence are linked from the Evidence Press release page. This briefing uses an AI-generated voice and is not additional scientific evidence.
